steps: Prophase: Chromatin condenses to form visible chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids joined at a centromere.
The nucleolus and nuclear membrane disappear, and spindle fibres form as the centrioles move towards opposite poles of the cell.
Metaphase: Chromosomes attach to spindle fibres at their centromeres and arrange themselves at the equator of the cell.
Anaphase: The centromeres divide, and the sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles of the cell.
Telophase: Chromatids reach the poles and become chromosomes; they uncoil, the spindle fibres disappear, and new nuclear membranes and nucleoli form around each set of chromosomes.
Mitosis produces two daughter nuclei containing the same number and kinds of chromosomes as the parent nucleus.
items.finalAnswer: Mitosis proceeds through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, producing two genetically identical daughter nuclei.

steps: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm to form two separate daughter cells after nuclear division.
In an animal cell, the cell membrane constricts inwards at the middle, forming a cleavage furrow.
The cleavage furrow deepens until the cytoplasm is divided and two daughter cells are separated.
In a plant cell, vesicles gather at the equator and fuse to form a cell plate.
The cell plate grows outwards until it joins the existing cell wall and separates the cytoplasm into two daughter cells.
items.finalAnswer: Animal cells divide by a cleavage furrow, while plant cells divide by formation of a cell plate; both processes separate the daughter cells.

steps: Prophase I: Chromosomes become visible, and each chromosome consists of two chromatids joined at a centromere.
Homologous chromosomes pair with each other to form pairs called bivalents.
Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange segments of genetic material; this process is called crossing over.
The nuclear membrane and nucleolus disappear, and spindle fibres form.
Metaphase I: Homologous chromosome pairs arrange themselves at the equator of the cell, and spindle fibres attach to their centromeres.
Anaphase I: Homologous chromosomes separate and move towards opposite poles of the cell.
The centromeres do not divide, so the sister chromatids of each chromosome remain attached.
Telophase I: The chromosomes reach the poles, and the cell divides to form two haploid cells; each chromosome still consists of two chromatids.
items.finalAnswer: In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes pair and may exchange segments, then separate to opposite poles while their centromeres remain undivided, forming two haploid cells.
